title: The dark night, again
hookLine: John of the Cross: God works in darkness, weaning us from feelings

lines: A CELL WITH ALMOST NO LIGHT.
cards: A tiny cell. Almost no light. Tradition says a Spanish friar named John was locked in a room like this by members of his own religious order, who didn't like his reforms.
No books. Bread and water. And in that darkness, tradition says, he began to compose poems in his head.

Out of that time, the story goes, came a poem that begins on a dark night, a soul slipping out of a quiet house, unseen, guided by no light except the one burning in the heart. We met this phrase in year one.
Today, a sharper question: what is the darkness for?

teach.b: John later wrote a long explanation of his poem, and at its center is a mother and a child. At first, he says, God treats a new believer like a mother nursing a baby: warm, sweet, easy. Prayer feels good.
Then, like any mother, God begins to wean the child.
The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so the child can grow up and eat real food. The Psalms already use the image: "my soul is even as a weaned child."
And Paul tells the Corinthians, "I have fed you with milk, and not with meat." Why wean at all? John says a soul can come to love the good feelings of prayer more than God.
So God gently removes the feelings. What's left, in his telling, if you stay, is a love that doesn't depend on getting something back. John was careful, too.

teach.h: NOT EVERY DRYNESS IS THE NIGHT.
teach.b: Not every dryness is this night, he wrote; some comes from sin, carelessness or sickness of body and mind, and he told guides to tell them apart.
Hold that next to a lesson from a few days ago: depression needs care and help, and naming something a dark night is no reason to skip it. And inside the night?
John's advice is simple: don't strain to force the old feelings back.
Stay quiet, with a loving attention, and let God work. The psalm says, "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." In the psalm, the night isn't empty to God.

how: Catholics honor John of the Cross as a saint and Doctor of the Church, and his poem and commentary are read by Christians of several churches; spiritual directors draw on his advice to help people tell a season of dryness in prayer apart from depression or neglect.

o: a time when God has left and won't come back
a punishment for praying with the wrong words
a season when prayer's sweetness goes so love can grow

games.q: the dark night — tap the pairs.
p: the psalm's picture of a quiet soul

s: John of the Cross says every dry spell in prayer is the dark night
he says dryness can also come from sin, carelessness or sickness, and guides should tell them apart.
John compares God to a mother weaning a child
the sweetness is taken away so the child can grow and eat real food.
John advises straining hard to bring the old feelings back
his advice is to stay quiet, with loving attention, and let God work.

games.q: you've prayed for years, and suddenly it feels like nothing. no warmth, no words. what does John of the Cross advise?
o: try harder to make the feelings come back.
stay quiet before God, with a loving attention, and let it work.
stop praying until the feeling returns.
games.why: John says not to strain after the old sweetness. stay quiet and attentive: in his telling, the night itself is doing the work.

practice: Close your eyes and let the darkness behind your eyelids be just what it is, with no special feeling, picture or answer to chase. Stay with a quiet, open attention, the way you'd sit in a dark room waiting for your eyes to adjust.
If you pray, rest there before God without words; if you don't, rest in the not-knowing.

wordCard.voice: The dark night. John of the Cross's name for the season when God takes away prayer's sweetness, as a mother weans a child, so love can grow.

carryVoice: Your line: night is working. For John, even the dark was going somewhere. See you tomorrow.
